title: Wood v. Lucy, Lady Duff-Gordon
shortTitle: Wood v. Lucy, Lady Duff Gordon
summary: The exclusive agency agreement carried an implied promise of reasonable efforts, avoiding an illusory-promise objection.
notes:
Court: Court of Appeals of New York (1917).

The assigned full contract in SEL has not been supplied. The casebook discusses reasonable efforts; UCC § 2-306(2) uses best efforts in its sales setting. Do not silently treat this licensing agreement as itself a sale of goods or erase the difference in wording.

sections.Parties: Wood, an exclusive commercial agent, sued Lucy, Lady Duff-Gordon, the fashion designer whose endorsement and designs had commercial value.
sections.Material Facts: Lucy gave Wood exclusive rights to arrange endorsements and market designs, in return for half the profits or revenues from the contemplated exploitation. The writing required accounting and addressed protection of intellectual-property interests. It did not expressly say that Wood would exert efforts. Wood alleged that Lucy made arrangements herself and withheld his share.
sections.Procedural History: The claim came before the New York Court of Appeals on the sufficiency of the complaint. The court reversed the Appellate Division and restored the Special Term ruling allowing the action to proceed. Three judges dissented without an opinion reproduced here. The court did not adjudicate final breach damages.
sections.Issue: Did the agreement fail for lack of consideration because Wood had made no express promise to work?
sections.Holding: No. The agreement, read as a whole, implied an obligation to use reasonable efforts to bring about the contemplated revenues.
sections.Reasoning: Exclusivity, compensation dependent on results, the promise to account, and the commercial purpose make the implied undertaking part of the bargain. A reading leaving Wood free to do nothing would frustrate the arrangement’s evident operation. The implied duty supplies an obligation for which Lucy exchanged her exclusive grant. This is an interpretive implication from this contract, not a rule that every missing promise must be invented to save a bargain.
